newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary's Horn may plan gradual reshuffle - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Hungary's Horn may plan gradual reshuffle - analysts.

text.p: Hungarian Prime Minister Gyula Horn's dismissal of his agricultural minister, the eleventh minister to depart in two years, could be part of a disguised reshuffle, political analysts said on Thursday.

"This could be part of a bigger issue," Istvan Stumpf, head of political science at the Hungarian Academy of Sciences told Reuters. "Horn could be trying to give a new face to his government for the new year."
Horn dismissed Agriculture Minister Laszlo Lakos on Wednesday saying that a change was needed in order to prepare Hungary's agriculture for European Union requirements.
The dismissal followed on the heels of the departure of Welfare Minister Gyorgy Szabo on Tuesday who resigned in protest at insufficient funds for the health service in 1997.

Both ministers were among a list of suggested changes reportedly put forward by a group of centrist Socialist MPs earlier this month. The list also included Justice Minister Pal Vastagh and Environment Minister Ferenc Baja.
The MPs said this was the last chance to bring in new faces before the run-up to new elections in the spring of 1998.
Horn immediately denied he was planning a reshuffle but political analyst Tibor Vidos, of the GJW consultancy, said he believed Horn would not have sacked Lakos without such party pressure.
"The coincidence is too strong to believe Horn was not influenced," Vidos told Reuters, adding that Horn did not introduce a complete reshuffle because it goes against his political instincts.
"Horn doesn't believe in wholesale reshuffles," he said. "He doesn't want to open too many fronts or fight too many battles at the same time -- he prefers to do these kinds of things one by one."

Lakos's dismissal was made easier by last week's decision by the National Association of Agricultural Producers to appeal to the Constitutional Court because of Lakos's failure to announce guaranteed procurement prices despite a law stipulating that such prices should be announced by October 1.
"Lakos has had a lot of criticism from professionals within agriculture -- there was a lot of dissatisfaction," said Stumpf.
However, Stumpf also believed that the sacking should not be taken in isolation.
"I don't think this is only the consequence of heavy criticism of the agricultural ministry," he said.
Vidos said that a tally of 10 changes of ministry heads and one change of minister without portfolio was not excessive in a country going through difficult economic times.

"Apart from personal differences with Horn, the departures come from ministries where conflict over budgetary allocations are greatest," he said. "We've had three finance ministers and we are about to to see a third welfare minister."
"At budget time ministers are very vulnerable."
